claim: Genes encoding glycosyltransferases can be under relatively high selection pressure, likely due to the involvement of the glycans synthesized in host-microbe interactions.
source: Genes encoding glycosyltransferases can be under relatively high selection pressure, likely due to the involvement of the glycans synthesized in host-microbe interactions.
evidence: This is stated as background knowledge in the abstract without specific experimental data or citations provided in this sentence.

claim: Ggta1 deletion shaped the composition of the gut microbiota.
source: We found that Ggta1 deletion shaped the composition of the gut microbiota.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1 showing differences in microbiota composition between Ggta1+/+ and Ggta1-/- mice.

claim: Ggta1 deletion shaped the microbiota via an immunoglobulin (Ig)-dependent mechanism, associated with targeting of αGal-expressing bacteria by IgA.
source: This occurred via an immunoglobulin (Ig)-dependent mechanism, associated with targeting of αGal-expressing bacteria by IgA.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figures 2 and 3 showing IgA targeting of αGal+ bacteria and Ig-dependent microbiota shaping.

claim: Systemic infection with an Ig-shaped microbiota inoculum elicited a less severe form of sepsis compared to infection with non-Ig-shaped microbiota.
source: Systemic infection with an Ig-shaped microbiota inoculum elicited a less severe form of sepsis compared to infection with non-Ig-shaped microbiota.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 4 showing differential survival and bacterial loads.

claim: In the absence of host αGal, antibodies can shape the microbiota towards lower pathogenicity.
source: This suggests that in the absence of host αGal, antibodies can shape the microbiota towards lower pathogenicity.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing reduced pathogenicity of Ig-shaped microbiota in Ggta1-/- mice.

claim: The observed reduction in microbiota pathogenicity upon Ggta1 deletion in mice may have contributed to increase the frequency of GGTA1 loss-of-function mutations in ancestral primates that gave rise to humans.
source: Given the fitness cost imposed by bacterial sepsis, we infer that the observed reduction in microbiota pathogenicity upon Ggta1 deletion in mice may have contributed to increase the frequency of GGTA1 loss-of-function mutations in ancestral primates that gave rise to humans.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about evolutionary implications based on the experimental findings in mice.

claim: Infectious diseases are a major driving force of natural selection.
source: As originally proposed by J.B.S. Haldane, infectious diseases are a major driving force of natural selection (Haldane, 1949), occasionally precipitating 'catastrophic-selection' events: the replacement of an entire, susceptible, parental population by mutant offspring that are resistant to a given infectious disease (Lewis, 1962).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Haldane (1949) and Lewis (1962).

claim: A catastrophic-selection event is proposed to have occurred during primate evolution between 20–30 million years ago, possibly due to the selective pressure exerted by an airborne, enveloped virus carrying αGal-like glycans.
source: Such an event is proposed to have occurred during primate evolution between 20–30 million‐years‐ago, possibly due to the selective pressure exerted by an airborne, enveloped virus carrying Galα1-3Galβ1-4GlcNAc (αGal)-like glycans (Galili, 2016; Galili, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Galili (2016) and Galili (2019).

claim: Loss of the α1,3-galactosyltransferase enzyme eliminated the expression of protein-bound αGal, allowing for immune targeting of this non-self glycan.
source: Loss of the α1,3-galactosyltransferase enzyme, encoded by GGTA1, eliminated the expression of protein-bound αGal, allowing for immune targeting of this non-self glycan (Galili et al., 1987).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Galili et al. (1987).

claim: Loss of GGTA1 function increased resistance to infection by αGal-expressing pathogens.
source: This increased resistance to infection by αGal-expressing pathogens (Repik et al., 1994; Takeuchi et al., 1996), including parasites of the Plasmodium spp. (Soares and Yilmaz, 2016; Yilmaz et al., 2014), which exerted a major impact on human evolution (Allison, 1954).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations including Repik et al. (1994), Takeuchi et al. (1996), Soares and Yilmaz (2016), Yilmaz et al. (2014), and Allison (1954).

claim: Loss of αGal from IgG-associated glycan structures increased IgG effector function and resistance to bacterial sepsis in mice.
source: Namely, loss of αGal from immunoglobulin (Ig)G-associated glycan structures increased IgG effector function and resistance to bacterial sepsis in mice (Singh et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Singh et al. (2021).

claim: Sepsis is a life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a deregulated response to infection that accounts for 20% of global human mortality.
source: Sepsis is a life-threatening organ dysfunction caused by a deregulated response to infection (Singer et al., 2016) that accounts for 20% of global human mortality (Rudd et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Singer et al. (2016) and Rudd et al. (2020).

claim: The pathogenesis of sepsis is modulated by stable host symbiotic associations with microbial communities composed of bacteria, fungi, and viruses, known as the microbiota.
source: The pathogenesis of sepsis is modulated by stable host symbiotic associations with microbial communities composed of bacteria, fungi, and viruses, known as the microbiota (Rudd et al., 2020; Vincent et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Rudd et al. (2020) and Vincent et al. (2009).

claim: Host-microbiota interactions provide a broad range of fitness advantages to the host.
source: While host-microbiota interactions provide a broad range of fitness advantages to the host (Lane-Petter, 1962; Vonaesch et al., 2018), these also carry fitness costs, for example, when bacterial pathobionts (Chow et al., 2011) translocate across host epithelial barriers to elicit the development of sepsis (Rudd et al., 2020; Vincent et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Lane-Petter (1962) and Vonaesch et al. (2018).

claim: Host-microbiota interactions carry fitness costs when bacterial pathobionts translocate across host epithelial barriers to elicit the development of sepsis.
source: While host-microbiota interactions provide a broad range of fitness advantages to the host (Lane-Petter, 1962; Vonaesch et al., 2018), these also carry fitness costs, for example, when bacterial pathobionts (Chow et al., 2011) translocate across host epithelial barriers to elicit the development of sepsis (Rudd et al., 2020; Vincent et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chow et al. (2011), Rudd et al. (2020), and Vincent et al. (2009).

claim: The immune system may have emerged, in part, to mitigate the pathogenic effects of the microbiota.
source: On the basis of this evolutionary trade-off (Stearns and Medzhitov, 2015), it has been argued that the immune system may have emerged, in part, to mitigate the pathogenic effects of the microbiota (Hooper et al., 2012; McFall-Ngai, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Stearns and Medzhitov (2015), Hooper et al. (2012), and McFall-Ngai (2007).

claim: Central to host defence strategy is the transepithelial secretion of copious amounts of IgA natural antibodies, which target immunogenic bacteria in the microbiota.
source: Central to this host defence strategy is the transepithelial secretion of copious amounts of IgA natural antibodies (NAb), which target immunogenic bacteria in the microbiota (Macpherson et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Macpherson et al. (2000).

claim: IgA recognize a broad but defined subset of immunogenic bacteria in the gut microbiota.
source: IgA recognize a broad but defined subset of immunogenic bacteria in the gut microbiota (Bunker et al., 2017; Bunker et al., 2015; Macpherson et al., 2000), exerting negative or positive selection pressure on these bacteria, shaping the microbiota composition, ecology, and potentially its pathogenicity (Kubinak and Round, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bunker et al. (2017), Bunker et al. (2015), and Macpherson et al. (2000).

claim: IgA exert negative or positive selection pressure on bacteria, shaping the microbiota composition, ecology, and potentially its pathogenicity.
source: IgA recognize a broad but defined subset of immunogenic bacteria in the gut microbiota (Bunker et al., 2017; Bunker et al., 2015; Macpherson et al., 2000), exerting negative or positive selection pressure on these bacteria, shaping the microbiota composition, ecology, and potentially its pathogenicity (Kubinak and Round, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Kubinak and Round (2016).

claim: Negative selection by IgA can occur when IgA limits bacterial growth.
source: Negative selection can occur, for example, when IgA limits bacterial growth (Moor et al., 2017), while positive selection can occur, for example, when IgA promotes bacterial interactions with the host, favoring bacterial retention, fitness, and colonization (Donaldson et al., 2018; McLoughlin et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Moor et al. (2017).

claim: Positive selection by IgA can occur when IgA promotes bacterial interactions with the host, favoring bacterial retention, fitness, and colonization.
source: Negative selection can occur, for example, when IgA limits bacterial growth (Moor et al., 2017), while positive selection can occur, for example, when IgA promotes bacterial interactions with the host, favoring bacterial retention, fitness, and colonization (Donaldson et al., 2018; McLoughlin et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Donaldson et al. (2018) and McLoughlin et al. (2016).

claim: IgA can interfere with cognate interactions between bacteria and tissue resident immune cells at epithelial barriers, regulating microbiota-specific immune responses, including the production of circulating IgM and IgG NAb.
source: Moreover, IgA can interfere with cognate interactions between bacteria and tissue resident immune cells at epithelial barriers, regulating microbiota-specific immune responses, including the production of circulating IgM and IgG NAb (Kamada et al., 2015; Zeng et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kamada et al. (2015) and Zeng et al. (2016).

claim: Ggta1-/- mice harbor a distinct microbiota composition to that of wild type (Ggta1+/+) mice.
source: We have previously established that Ggta1-/- mice harbor a distinct microbiota composition to that of wild type (Ggta1+/+) mice (Singh et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Singh et al. (2021) and by data in Figure 1.

claim: There is an increase in Proteobacteria, Tenericutes, and Verrucomicrobia as well as a reduction in Bacterioidetes and Deferribacteres phyla in Ggta1-/- mice compared to Ggta1+/+ mice.
source: This is illustrated by the relative abundance of specific bacterial taxa, such as an increase in Proteobacteria, Tenericutes, and Verrucomicrobia as well as a reduction in Bacterioidetes and Deferribacteres phyla in Ggta1-/- mice compared to Ggta1+/+ mice (Figure 1A, Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2; Singh et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2, as well as citation to Singh et al. (2021).

claim: The relative increase of Proteobacteria in the gut microbiota of Ggta1-/- mice was not associated with the development of histological lesions in the gastrointestinal tract.
source: The relative increase of Proteobacteria, a phylum containing several strains associated with pathogenic behavior, in the gut microbiota of Ggta1-/- mice was not, however, associated with the development of histological lesions in the gastrointestinal tract (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Absence of intestinal inflammation in Ggta1-/- mice was assessed by quantification of fecal lipocalin-2 (Lcn-2).
source: Absence of intestinal inflammation was further assessed by quantification of fecal lipocalin-2 (Lcn-2) (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B; Chassaing et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B and citation to Chassaing et al. (2012).

claim: There were no histopathological lesions in the liver, lungs, kidney, and spleen of Ggta1-/- mice.
source: There were also no histopathological lesions in the liver, lungs, kidney, and spleen (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C), suggesting that Ggta1-/- mice maintain symbiotic interactions with these pathobionts, without compromising organismal homeostasis.
evidence: This claim is supported by histological data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claim: Ggta1-/- mice maintain symbiotic interactions with pathobionts without compromising organismal homeostasis.
source: There were also no histopathological lesions in the liver, lungs, kidney, and spleen (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C), suggesting that Ggta1-/- mice maintain symbiotic interactions with these pathobionts, without compromising organismal homeostasis.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the absence of histopathological lesions shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C.

claim: The microbiota composition of F1 Ggta1+/- as well as F2 Ggta1+/+ and Ggta1-/- mice diverged from that of the original F0 Ggta1+/+ mice.
source: The microbiota composition of F1 Ggta1+/- well as F2 Ggta1+/+ and Ggta1-/- mice diverged from that of the original F0 Ggta1+/+ mice (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The microbiota composition was indistinguishable in F2 Ggta1+/+ and Ggta1-/- littermates.
source: While indistinguishable in F2 Ggta1+/+ and Ggta1-/- littermates (Figure 1C; Singh et al., 2021), the microbiota composition diverged between Ggta1+/+ and Ggta1-/- mice in F3 (Figure 1D), F4 (Figure 1E) and F5 (Figure 1F) generations, suggesting that the Ggta1 genotype per se alters microbiota composition.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 1C and citation to Singh et al. (2021).

claim: The microbiota composition diverged between Ggta1+/+ and Ggta1-/- mice in F3, F4 and F5 generations.
source: While indistinguishable in F2 Ggta1+/+ and Ggta1-/- littermates (Figure 1C; Singh et al., 2021), the microbiota composition diverged between Ggta1+/+ and Ggta1-/- mice in F3 (Figure 1D), F4 (Figure 1E) and F5 (Figure 1F) generations, suggesting that the Ggta1 genotype per se alters microbiota composition.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figures 1D, 1E, and 1F.

claim: The Ggta1 genotype per se alters microbiota composition.
source: While indistinguishable in F2 Ggta1+/+ and Ggta1-/- littermates (Figure 1C; Singh et al., 2021), the microbiota composition diverged between Ggta1+/+ and Ggta1-/- mice in F3 (Figure 1D), F4 (Figure 1E) and F5 (Figure 1F) generations, suggesting that the Ggta1 genotype per se alters microbiota composition.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the divergence of microbiota composition across generations shown in Figures 1D-F.

claim: There was an enrichment of some bacterial taxa, such as Helicobactereaceae, in the microbiota of F2 to F5 Ggta1-/- and Ggta1+/+ mice, despite the absence of these bacteria in the original F0 Ggta1+/+ microbiota.
source: There was an enrichment of some bacterial taxa, such as Helicobactereaceae, in the microbiota of F2 to F5 Ggta1-/- and Ggta1+/+ mice (Figure 1—figure supplement 4), despite the absence of these bacteria in the original F0 Ggta1+/+ microbiota (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: The Ggta1 genotype shapes the gut microbiota composition via a process that is probably influenced by colonization by environmental pathobionts.
source: This suggests that the Ggta1 genotype shapes the gut microbiota composition via a process that is probably influenced by colonization by environmental pathobionts (Gálvez et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the enrichment of Helicobactereaceae in later generations, supported by citation to Gálvez et al. (2017).

claim: The relative levels of microbiota-reactive circulating IgA were higher in Ggta1-/- vs. Ggta1+/+ mice maintained under specific pathogen-free (SPF) but not germ-free (GF) conditions.
source: In keeping with this notion, the relative levels of microbiota-reactive circulating IgA were higher in Ggta1-/- vs. Ggta1+/+ mice, maintained under specific pathogen-free (SPF) but not germ-free (GF) conditions (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Under SPF conditions, Ggta1-/- mice had similar levels of secreted and circulating total IgA, compared to Ggta1+/+ mice.
source: Under SPF conditions, Ggta1-/- mice had similar levels of secreted (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) and circulating (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) total IgA, compared to Ggta1+/+ mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and 1B.

claim: Total IgA levels were reduced to a similar extent under GF conditions in both Ggta1-/- and Ggta1+/+ mice.
source: These were reduced to a similar extent under GF conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B), suggesting that Ggta1 deletion enhances microbiota-specific IgA responses without interfering with total IgA.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Ggta1 deletion enhances microbiota-specific IgA responses without interfering with total IgA.
source: These were reduced to a similar extent under GF conditions (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B), suggesting that Ggta1 deletion enhances microbiota-specific IgA responses without interfering with total IgA.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A and B showing similar total IgA levels but different microbiota-reactive IgA levels.

claim: Colonization of GF Ggta1-/- mice with the microbiota from Ggta1-/- mice elicited the production of higher levels of microbiota-reactive circulating IgA, compared to GF Ggta1+/+ mice colonized by the same microbiota.
source: In further support of the notion that Ggta1 deletion modulates the production of microbiota-specific IgA, colonization of GF Ggta1-/- mice with the microbiota from Ggta1-/- mice elicited the production of higher levels of microbiota-reactive circulating IgA, compared to GF Ggta1+/+ mice colonized by the same microbiota (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: The difference in microbiota-reactive IgA was not observed upon colonization of GF Ggta1-/- vs. Ggta1+/+ mice by a microbiota isolated from Ggta1+/+ mice.
source: This difference was not observed upon colonization of GF Ggta1-/- vs. Ggta1+/+ mice by a microbiota isolated from Ggta1+/+ mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The enhanced microbiota-reactive IgA response of Ggta1-/- vs. Ggta1+/+ mice is induced by immunogenic bacteria present specifically in the microbiota of Ggta1-/- mice.
source: This suggests that the enhanced microbiota-reactive IgA response of Ggta1-/- vs. Ggta1+/+ mice is induced by immunogenic bacteria present specifically in the microbiota of Ggta1-/- mice.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the differential IgA responses upon colonization with different microbiota sources.

claim: The levels of circulating IgA were reduced in Tcrb-/-Ggta1-/- mice lacking α/β T cells, when compared to Ggta1-/- mice.
source: Of note, the levels of circulating IgA were reduced in Tcrb-/-Ggta1-/- mice lacking α/β T cells, when compared to Ggta1-/- mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), suggesting that the production of circulating IgA NAb in Ggta1-/- mice occurs, in part, via a T-cell-dependent mechanism, which is consistent with previous reports in Ggta1+/+ mice (Bunker et al., 2017; Fagarasan et al., 2010; Macpherson et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and citations to Bunker et al. (2017), Fagarasan et al. (2010), and Macpherson et al. (2000).

claim: The production of circulating IgA NAb in Ggta1-/- mice occurs, in part, via a T-cell-dependent mechanism.
source: Of note, the levels of circulating IgA were reduced in Tcrb-/-Ggta1-/- mice lacking α/β T cells, when compared to Ggta1-/- mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 1D), suggesting that the production of circulating IgA NAb in Ggta1-/- mice occurs, in part, via a T-cell-dependent mechanism, which is consistent with previous reports in Ggta1+/+ mice (Bunker et al., 2017; Fagarasan et al., 2010; Macpherson et al., 2000).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the reduced IgA levels in T cell-deficient mice, supported by data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1D and citations.

claim: Several bacteria in the human gut microbiota carry genes orthologous to the mammalian α1,3-galactosyltransferase.
source: Consistent with a number of bacteria in the human gut microbiota carrying genes orthologous to the mammalian α1,3-galactosyltransferase (Montassier et al., 2019), several human probiotic bacteria expressed αGal-like glycans at the cell surface when cultured in vitro (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Montassier et al. (2019) and data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Several human probiotic bacteria expressed αGal-like glycans at the cell surface when cultured in vitro.
source: Consistent with a number of bacteria in the human gut microbiota carrying genes orthologous to the mammalian α1,3-galactosyltransferase (Montassier et al., 2019), several human probiotic bacteria expressed αGal-like glycans at the cell surface when cultured in vitro (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Approximately 20% of the bacteria in the small intestine of Ggta1+/+ mice expressed αGal-like glycans at the cell surface.
source: Subsequent in vivo analyses demonstrated that approximately 20% of the bacteria in the small intestine of Ggta1+/+ mice expressed αGal-like glycans at the cell surface (Figure 2D,E, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D, 2E, and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Nearly 30% of αGal+ bacteria in the small intestine were immunogenic, as defined by the detection of surface-bound IgA.
source: Nearly 30% of these αGal+ bacteria were immunogenic (Figure 2D,E), as defined by the detection of surface-bound IgA (Palm et al., 2014), which predominantly targets bacteria in the small intestine (Bunker et al., 2017; Bunker et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D and 2E, and citations to Palm et al. (2014), Bunker et al. (2017), and Bunker et al. (2015).

claim: IgA+αGal+ bacteria accounted for roughly 50% of all the immunogenic (IgA+) bacteria in the small intestine.
source: These IgA+αGal+ bacteria accounted for roughly 50% of all the immunogenic (IgA+) bacteria in the small intestine (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D and 2E.

claim: Ggta1-/- mice harbored a relatively lower percentage of immunogenic IgA+αGal+ bacteria in the small intestine, when compared to Ggta1+/+ mice.
source: Ggta1-/- mice harbored a relatively lower percentage of immunogenic IgA+αGal+ bacteria in the small intestine, when compared to Ggta1+/+ mice (Figure 2D,E), while the percentage of immunogenic IgA+ bacteria was similar in Ggta1-/- vs. Ggta1+/+ mice (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D and 2E.

claim: The percentage of immunogenic IgA+ bacteria was similar in Ggta1-/- vs. Ggta1+/+ mice.
source: Ggta1-/- mice harbored a relatively lower percentage of immunogenic IgA+αGal+ bacteria in the small intestine, when compared to Ggta1+/+ mice (Figure 2D,E), while the percentage of immunogenic IgA+ bacteria was similar in Ggta1-/- vs. Ggta1+/+ mice (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D and 2E.

claim: Induction of dysbiosis by streptomycin increased the levels of circulating αGal-specific IgM and IgG in Igha-/-Ggta1-/- vs. Igha+/+Ggta1-/- mice.
source: Induction of dysbiosis, by streptomycin, increased the levels of circulating αGal-specific IgM and IgG in Igha-/-Ggta1-/- vs. Igha+/+Ggta1-/- mice (Figure 2F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2F and 2G.

claim: The IgA response of Ggta1-/- mice reduces systemic IgM and IgG responses against antigens expressed by bacteria in the microbiota.
source: This illustrates again that the IgA response of Ggta1-/- mice is distinct from that of Ggta1+/+ mice, reducing systemic IgM and IgG responses against antigens expressed by bacteria in the microbiota, as illustrated for αGal-like glycans.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the increased systemic IgM and IgG in IgA-deficient mice shown in Figure 2F and 2G.

claim: IgA prevents αGal+ bacteria or bacterial products associated to αGal from translocating across epithelial barriers and inducing systemic immune responses against this glycan.
source: Presumably this occurs via a mechanism whereby IgA prevents αGal+ bacteria or bacterial products associated to αGal from translocating across epithelial barriers and inducing systemic immune responses against this glycan.
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism proposed to explain the reduced systemic antibody responses in the presence of IgA.

claim: Maintenance of microbiota composition across generations is sustained via maternal IgG transfer to the offspring through the placenta during the fetal period, and maternal IgM, IgG and IgA transfer via lactation during the neonatal period.
source: Maintenance of microbiota composition across generations is sustained via maternal IgG transfer to the offspring through the placenta during the fetal period, and maternal IgM, IgG and IgA transfer via lactation during the neonatal period (Gensollen et al., 2016; Koch et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gensollen et al. (2016) and Koch et al. (2016).

claim: Over time, newborns generate IgA that target immunogenic bacteria in the microbiota, shaping its composition throughout adult life.
source: Over time, newborns generate IgA that target immunogenic bacteria in the microbiota (McLoughlin et al., 2016; Moor et al., 2017), shaping its composition throughout adult life (Kawamoto et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to McLoughlin et al. (2016), Moor et al. (2017), and Kawamoto et al. (2014).

claim: F2 Igh-J+/+Ggta1+/+, Igh-J+/+Ggta1-/-, Igh-J-/-Ggta1+/+ and Igh-J-/-Ggta1-/- mice harbored a microbiota composition indistinguishable among the genotypes.
source: Crossing of F0 Igh-J+/+Ggta1+/+ (female) with Igh-J-/-Ggta1-/- (male) mice produced F1 Igh-J+/-Ggta1+/-mice, which were interbred to generate F2 Igh-J+/+Ggta1+/+, Igh-J+/+Ggta1-/-, Igh-J-/-Ggta1+/+ and Igh-J-/-Ggta1-/- mice, harboring a microbiota composition indistinguishable among the genotypes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Maternal Ig transfer predominates over offspring Ig production in shaping the offspring microbiota, regardless of the genotype.
source: Consistent with our previous observations (Figure 1C; Singh et al., 2021), this suggests that maternal Ig transfer predominates over offspring Ig production in shaping the offspring microbiota, regardless of the genotype (Ubeda et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the indistinguishable microbiota composition in F2 mice, supported by citation to Ubeda et al. (2012) and Singh et al. (2021).

claim: There was a marked separation of the microbiota community structure between F3 Igh-J+/+Ggta1-/- vs. Igh-J+/+Ggta1+/+ mice, as assessed by Principal Coordinate Analyses for Weighted and Unweighted Unifrac.
source: Consistent with our previous observations (Figure 1), there was a marked separation of the microbiota community structure between F3 Igh-J+/+Ggta1-/- vs. Igh-J+/+Ggta1+/+ mice, as assessed by Principal Coordinate Analyses (PCA) for Weighted and Unweighted Unifrac (Figure 3B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B and 3C.

claim: Ggta1 deletion shapes both high and low abundant taxa present in the microbiota when maternal and/or offspring-derived antibodies are present.
source: Considering that Weighted Unifrac accounts for the relative abundance of the bacterial taxa while Unweighted Unifrac accounts for only the presence or absence of the taxa in the microbial community (Lozupone and Knight, 2005), they represent differences exerted by high and low abundant bacterial taxa respectively. This suggests that Ggta1 deletion shapes both high and low abundant taxa present in the microbiota when maternal and/or offspring-derived antibodies (i.e. Ig) are present.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the PCA data in Figure 3B and 3C, supported by citation to Lozupone and Knight (2005).

claim: The microbiota from Igh-J+/+Ggta1-/- mice was enriched in specific bacterial taxa, including Proteobacteria, as compared to the microbiota from Igh-J+/+Ggta1+/+ mice.
source: LefSe analysis showed that the microbiota from Igh-J+/+Ggta1-/- mice was enriched in specific bacterial taxa, including Proteobacteria, as compared to the microbiota from Igh-J+/+Ggta1+/+ mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Ggta1 deletion favors gut colonization by pathobionts in an Ig-dependent manner.
source: This suggests that Ggta1 deletion favors gut colonization by pathobionts in an Ig-dependent manner.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the enrichment of Proteobacteria in Igh-J+/+Ggta1-/- mice.

claim: In the absence of Ig (Igh-J-/-), there were no differences in the microbiota composition of F3 Igh-J-/-Ggta1-/- vs. Igh-J-/-Ggta1+/+ mice, as assessed by PCA for Weighted Unifrac.
source: In the absence of Ig (Igh-J-/-), there were no differences in the microbiota composition of F3 Igh-J-/-Ggta1-/- vs. Igh-J-/-Ggta1+/+ mice, as assessed by PCA for Weighted Unifrac (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Shaping of highly abundant taxa in the microbiota of Ggta1-/- vs. Ggta1+/+ mice occurs via an Ig-dependent mechanism.
source: This suggests that shaping of highly abundant taxa in the microbiota of Ggta1-/- vs. Ggta1+/+ mice occurs via an Ig-dependent mechanism.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lack of differences in Weighted Unifrac in the absence of Ig shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The microbiota composition of F3 Igh-J-/-Ggta1-/- mice remained distinct from that of Igh-J-/-Ggta1+/+ mice, as assessed by PCA for Unweighted Unifrac.
source: In contrast, the microbiota composition of F3 Igh-J-/-Ggta1-/- mice remained distinct from that of Igh-J-/-Ggta1+/+ mice, as assessed by PCA for Unweighted Unifrac (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Shaping of low abundance bacterial taxa in the microbiota of Ggta1-/- vs. Ggta1+/+ mice occurs in an Ig-independent manner.
source: This suggests that shaping of low abundance bacterial taxa in the microbiota of Ggta1-/- vs. Ggta1+/+ mice occurs in an Ig-independent manner.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the persistent differences in Unweighted Unifrac even in the absence of Ig shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The Weighted Unifrac distance of microbiota from Igh-J+/+Ggta1-/- vs. Igh-J-/-Ggta1-/- mice was higher than that from Igh-J+/+Ggta1+/+ vs. Igh-J-/-Ggta1+/+ mice.
source: The Weighted Unifrac distance of microbiota from Igh-J+/+Ggta1-/- vs. Igh-J-/-Ggta1-/- mice was higher than that from Igh-J+/+Ggta1+/+ vs. Igh-J-/-Ggta1+/+ mice (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The relative impact of Ig on the gut microbiota community structure exerted by highly abundant bacterial taxa is enhanced in Ggta1-/- vs. Ggta1+/+ mice.
source: This suggests that the relative impact of Ig on the gut microbiota community structure exerted by highly abundant bacterial taxa is enhanced in Ggta1-/- vs. Ggta1+/+ mice.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the higher Weighted Unifrac distance in Ggta1-/- mice shown in Figure 3D.

claim: There was an enhanced Ig-dependent enrichment of several bacterial taxa in the microbiota of Ggta1-/- mice, compared to that of Ggta1+/+ mice.
source: This was confirmed by LefSe analysis showing an enhanced Ig-dependent enrichment of several bacterial taxa in the microbiota of Ggta1-/- mice (Figure 3E–F), compared to that of Ggta1+/+ mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3E-F and Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The Unweighted Unifrac distance of Igh-J+/+Ggta1+/+ vs. Igh-J-/-Ggta1+/+ mice was higher compared to Igh-J+/+Ggta1-/- vs. Igh-J-/-Ggta1-/- mice.
source: In contrast, the Unweighted Unifrac distance of Igh-J+/+Ggta1+/+ vs. Igh-J-/-Ggta1+/+ mice was higher compared to Igh-J+/+Ggta1-/- vs. Igh-J-/-Ggta1-/- mice (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The relative impact of Ig on the microbiota community structure of low abundant bacterial taxa is less pronounced for Ggta1-/- vs. Ggta1+/+ mice.
source: This suggests that the relative impact of Ig on the microbiota community structure of low abundant bacterial taxa is less pronounced for Ggta1-/- vs. Ggta1+/+ mice.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lower Unweighted Unifrac distance in Ggta1-/- mice shown in Figure 3D.

claim: The gut microbiota from Igh-J-/-Ggta1-/- mice, lacking Ig, was enriched with Helicobactereaceae family from Proteobacteria phylum as compared to Igh-J+/+Ggta1-/- mice expressing Ig.
source: In strong support of this notion, the gut microbiota from Igh-J-/-Ggta1-/- mice, lacking Ig, was enriched with Helicobactereaceae family from Proteobacteria phylum as compared to Igh-J+/+Ggta1-/- mice expressing Ig (Figure 3E,F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3E and 3F.

claim: The gut microbiota of Rag2-/-Ggta1-/- mice, lacking adaptive immunity, is highly enriched in Proteobacteria, including Helicobacter.
source: This is consistent with our previous finding that the gut microbiota of Rag2-/-Ggta1-/- mice, lacking adaptive immunity, is highly enriched in Proteobacteria, including Helicobacter (Singh et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Singh et al. (2021).

claim: The enrichment of Helicobactereaceae was not observed in Igh-J-/-Ggta1+/+ vs. Igh-J+/+Ggta1+/+ mice.
source: Of note, this was not observed in Igh-J-/-Ggta1+/+ vs. Igh-J+/+Ggta1+/+ mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D.

claim: The absence of host αGal favors colonization of the gut microbiota by pathobionts, the expansion of which is restrained by Ig.
source: These data suggest that the absence of host αGal favors colonization of the gut microbiota by pathobionts, the expansion of which is restrained by Ig.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the enrichment of Helicobactereaceae in Ig-deficient Ggta1-/- mice but not in Ggta1+/+ mice.

claim: Ggta1-/- mice were protected against systemic infections by a cecal inoculum isolated from Rag2-/-Ggta1-/- mice.
source: Ggta1-/- mice were protected against systemic infections (i.p.) by a cecal inoculum isolated from Rag2-/-Ggta1-/- mice, reflecting a microbiota not shaped by Ig (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Ggta1 deletion enhances protection against systemic bacterial infections via a mechanism involving IgG NAb.
source: This is consistent with our previous finding showing Ggta1 deletion enhances protection against systemic bacterial infections (i.p.) via a mechanism involving IgG NAb (Singh et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Singh et al. (2021).

claim: Ggta1-/- mice were protected against a systemic infection by a cecal inoculum isolated from Ggta1-/- mice.
source: Moreover, Ggta1-/- mice were also protected against a systemic infection (i.p.) by a cecal inoculum isolated from Ggta1-/- mice, reflecting their own Ig-shaped microbiota (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Ggta1-/- mice are protected against cecal ligation and puncture.
source: This is in keeping with the previously shown enhanced protection of Ggta1-/- mice against cecal ligation and puncture (Singh et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Singh et al. (2021).

claim: Igh-J-/-Ggta1-/- mice lacking B cells remained protected against systemic infections by the cecal inoculum isolated from Ggta1-/- mice.
source: Surprisingly Igh-J-/-Ggta1-/- mice lacking B cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), Tcrb-/-Ggta1-/- mice lacking α/β T cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D) and Rag2-/-Ggta1-/- mice lacking B and T cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E) remained protected against systemic infections by the cecal inoculum isolated from Ggta1-/- mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Tcrb-/-Ggta1-/- mice lacking α/β T cells remained protected against systemic infections by the cecal inoculum isolated from Ggta1-/- mice.
source: Surprisingly Igh-J-/-Ggta1-/- mice lacking B cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), Tcrb-/-Ggta1-/- mice lacking α/β T cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D) and Rag2-/-Ggta1-/- mice lacking B and T cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E) remained protected against systemic infections by the cecal inoculum isolated from Ggta1-/- mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Rag2-/-Ggta1-/- mice lacking B and T cells remained protected against systemic infections by the cecal inoculum isolated from Ggta1-/- mice.
source: Surprisingly Igh-J-/-Ggta1-/- mice lacking B cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), Tcrb-/-Ggta1-/- mice lacking α/β T cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D) and Rag2-/-Ggta1-/- mice lacking B and T cells (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E) remained protected against systemic infections by the cecal inoculum isolated from Ggta1-/- mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: The IgG-dependent mechanism that protects Ggta1-/- mice from a systemic infection by a cecal inoculum isolated from Rag2-/-Ggta1-/- mice is distinct from that protecting Ggta1-/- mice from a systemic infection by their own cecal inoculum.
source: This suggests that the previously described IgG-dependent mechanism that protects Ggta1-/- mice from a systemic infection by a cecal inoculum isolated from Rag2-/-Ggta1-/- mice (Singh et al., 2021) is distinct from that protecting Ggta1-/- mice from a systemic infection by their own cecal inoculum.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the protection observed in adaptive immune-deficient mice, supported by citation to Singh et al. (2021).

claim: Rag2-/-Ggta1-/- mice remained protected against systemic infections by the cecal inoculum isolated from Ggta1-/- mice, while succumbing to a systemic infection by a cecal inoculum isolated from Rag2-/-Ggta1-/- mice.
source: Rag2-/-Ggta1-/- mice remained protected against systemic infections by the cecal inoculum isolated from Ggta1-/- mice, while succumbing to a systemic infection by a cecal inoculum isolated from Rag2-/-Ggta1-/- mice (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A and 4B.

claim: Lethality from systemic infection with Rag2-/-Ggta1-/- cecal inoculum was associated with a 10^6–10^7-fold increase in bacterial load.
source: Lethality was associated with a 106–107-fold increase in bacterial load (Figure 4C), suggesting that the Ig-shaped microbiota of Ggta1-/- mice is less pathogenic, when compared to the non-Ig-shaped microbiota from Rag2-/-Ggta1-/- mice.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The Ig-shaped microbiota of Ggta1-/- mice is less pathogenic, when compared to the non-Ig-shaped microbiota from Rag2-/-Ggta1-/- mice.
source: Lethality was associated with a 106–107-fold increase in bacterial load (Figure 4C), suggesting that the Ig-shaped microbiota of Ggta1-/- mice is less pathogenic, when compared to the non-Ig-shaped microbiota from Rag2-/-Ggta1-/- mice.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the differential survival and bacterial loads shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: Rag2-/-Ggta1+/+ mice succumbed to the same extent to systemic infection with a cecal inoculum isolated from either Rag2+/+Ggta1+/+ vs. Rag2-/-Ggta1+/+ mice.
source: However, Rag2-/-Ggta1+/+ mice succumbed to the same extent to systemic infection (i.p.) with a cecal inoculum isolated from either Rag2+/+Ggta1+/+ vs. Rag2-/-Ggta1+/+ mice (Figure 4D–E), developing similar bacterial loads (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4D-E.

claim: Rag2-/-Ggta1+/+ mice developed similar bacterial loads upon infection with cecal inocula from Rag2+/+Ggta1+/+ vs. Rag2-/-Ggta1+/+ mice.
source: However, Rag2-/-Ggta1+/+ mice succumbed to the same extent to systemic infection (i.p.) with a cecal inoculum isolated from either Rag2+/+Ggta1+/+ vs. Rag2-/-Ggta1+/+ mice (Figure 4D–E), developing similar bacterial loads (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: The mechanism via which the adaptive immune system of Ggta1-/- mice shapes and reduces the pathogenicity of its microbiota is not operational in Ggta1+/+ mice.
source: This suggests that the mechanism via which the adaptive immune system of Ggta1-/- mice shapes and reduces the pathogenicity of its microbiota is not operational in Ggta1+/+ mice.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lack of differential pathogenicity in Ggta1+/+ mice shown in Figure 4D-F.

claim: Depletion of Ly6C+/Ly6G+ myeloid cells using an anti-GR1 monoclonal Ab increased the susceptibility of Ggta1-/- mice to systemic infection by their cecal inoculum.
source: Depletion of Ly6C+/Ly6G+ myeloid cells (i.e. polymorphonuclear cells and inflammatory monocytes) using an anti-GR1 monoclonal Ab (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F; Daley et al., 2008) increased the susceptibility of Ggta1-/- mice to systemic infection by their cecal inoculum (Figure 4G).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4G and Figure 4—figure supplement 1F, and citation to Daley et al. (2008).

claim: Depletion of Ly6C+/Ly6G+ myeloid cells was associated with a 10^2–10^5-fold increase in bacterial load, compared to control Ggta1-/- mice.
source: This was associated with a 102–105-fold increase in bacterial load, compared to control Ggta1-/- mice (Figure 4H).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4H.

claim: Monocyte/macrophage depletion by Clodronate liposomes failed to compromise the survival of Ggta1-/- mice upon infection by the cecal inoculum.
source: Of note, monocyte/macrophage depletion by Clodronate liposomes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1G; Sunderkötter et al., 2004) failed to compromise the survival of Ggta1-/- mice upon infection by the same cecal inoculum (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1H and Figure 4—figure supplement 1G, and citation to Sunderkötter et al. (2004).

claim: Polymorphonuclear cells are essential for resistance against systemic infection emanating from the less pathogenic Ig-shaped microbiota of Ggta1-/- mice.
source: This suggests that polymorphonuclear cells are essential for resistance against systemic infection emanating from the less pathogenic Ig-shaped microbiota of Ggta1-/- mice.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the differential effects of neutrophil vs. macrophage depletion shown in Figure 4G-H and Figure 4—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Loss-of-function mutations in genes encoding glycosyltransferases can provide fitness advantages against infection but can compromise the physiologic functions of the eliminated self-glycan.
source: While loss-of-function mutations in genes encoding glycosyltransferases can provide fitness advantages against infection, these can compromise the physiologic functions of the eliminated self-glycan, as illustrated by the occurrence of reproductive senescence upon Ggta1 deletion in mice (Singh et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Singh et al. (2021).

claim: Reproductive senescence occurs upon Ggta1 deletion in mice.
source: While loss-of-function mutations in genes encoding glycosyltransferases can provide fitness advantages against infection, these can compromise the physiologic functions of the eliminated self-glycan, as illustrated by the occurrence of reproductive senescence upon Ggta1 deletion in mice (Singh et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Singh et al. (2021).

claim: Loss-of-function mutations in glycosyltransferase genes are rare, and in some cases unique, to the human lineage.
source: In an evolutionary context, such a trade-off could explain why loss-of-function mutations in these genes are rare, and in some cases unique, to the human lineage.
evidence: This is an inference based on evolutionary reasoning about the rarity of such mutations.

claim: Loss of CMP-N-acetylneuraminic acid hydroxylase (CMAH) function eliminated expression of the sialic acid, N-glycolylneuraminic acid (Neu5Gc), in humans.
source: The latter is illustrated by the loss of CMP-N-acetylneuraminic acid hydroxylase (CMAH) function, which eliminated expression of the sialic acid, N-glycolylneuraminic acid (Neu5Gc), in humans (Ghaderi et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Ghaderi et al. (2011).

claim: Co-evolution of ancestral hominids with commensal bacteria in their microbiota is thought to have provided a series of fitness advantages including optimization of nutrient intake from diet, regulation of different aspects of organismal metabolism or colonization resistance against pathogenic bacteria.
source: Co-evolution of ancestral hominids with commensal bacteria in their microbiota (Dethlefsen et al., 2007; Huttenhower et al., 2012; Moeller et al., 2016), is thought to have provided a series of fitness advantages including, among others, optimization of nutrient intake from diet, regulation of different aspects of organismal metabolism or colonization resistance against pathogenic bacteria (Buffie and Pamer, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dethlefsen et al. (2007), Huttenhower et al. (2012), Moeller et al. (2016), and Buffie and Pamer (2013).

claim: The loss of αGal expression, as it occurred during primate evolution, might have exerted a major impact on the nature of symbiotic associations with the microbiota.
source: Here we propose that the loss of αGal expression, as it occurred during primate evolution, might have exerted a major impact on the nature of these symbiotic associations.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the experimental findings in mice.

claim: Mutations altering the expression of human ABO blood group glycans are associated with shaping of the bacterial composition of the gut microbiota.
source: While our studies do not provide direct evidence that the loss of αGal played a major role in shaping the microbiota composition of Old- vs. New World primates, this notion is supported, indirectly, by the recent finding that mutations altering the expression of human ABO blood group glycans are associated with shaping of the bacterial composition of the gut microbiota (Rühlemann et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Rühlemann et al. (2021).

claim: Host 'αGal-like' glycans shape the microbiota composition of mice and primates, including that of humans.
source: In light of the structural similarity between the human B blood group (i.e. Galα1-3(Fucα1-2)Galβ1-4GlcNAcβ1-R), and αGal (i.e. Galα1-3Galβ1-4GlcNAcβ1-R) glycans, our findings probably reflect a general mechanism whereby host 'αGal-like' glycans shape the microbiota composition of mice and primates, including that of humans.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on structural similarity and experimental findings.

claim: A relatively large proportion of probiotic bacteria as well as bacteria present in the mouse microbiota express αGal-like glycans at the cell surface.
source: Consistent with this notion, a relatively large proportion of probiotic bacteria as well as bacteria present in the mouse microbiota express αGal-like glycans at the cell surface (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2.

claim: About 30% of αGal+ bacteria carry IgA at the cell surface in the mouse microbiota and are considered as immunogenic.
source: About 30% of these carry IgA at the cell surface in the mouse microbiota and, as such, are considered as immunogenic (Palm et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 2 and citation to Palm et al. (2014).

claim: Ggta1 deletion probably broadens bacterial recognition by IgA to include immunogenic αGal+ bacteria, which are presumably eliminated.
source: This suggests that Ggta1 deletion probably broadens bacterial recognition by IgA to include immunogenic αGal+ bacteria, which as a result are probably purged from the microbiota.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the reduced proportion of IgA+αGal+ bacteria in Ggta1-/- mice.

claim: IgA can target αGal-like glycans and modulate bacterial pathogenicity.
source: Of note, these are not mutually exclusive possibilities since: (i) IgA can target αGal-like glycans and modulate bacterial pathogenicity (Hamadeh et al., 1995), (ii) IgA are poly-reactive and can target common antigens expressed by bacteria (Bunker et al., 2017; Bunker et al., 2015) and (iii) αGal-reactive antibodies present a degree of poly-reactivity against non-αGal related bacterial epitopes (Bernth Jensen et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hamadeh et al. (1995).

claim: IgA are poly-reactive and can target common antigens expressed by bacteria.
source: Of note, these are not mutually exclusive possibilities since: (i) IgA can target αGal-like glycans and modulate bacterial pathogenicity (Hamadeh et al., 1995), (ii) IgA are poly-reactive and can target common antigens expressed by bacteria (Bunker et al., 2017; Bunker et al., 2015) and (iii) αGal-reactive antibodies present a degree of poly-reactivity against non-αGal related bacterial epitopes (Bernth Jensen et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bunker et al. (2017) and Bunker et al. (2015).

claim: αGal-reactive antibodies present a degree of poly-reactivity against non-αGal related bacterial epitopes.
source: Of note, these are not mutually exclusive possibilities since: (i) IgA can target αGal-like glycans and modulate bacterial pathogenicity (Hamadeh et al., 1995), (ii) IgA are poly-reactive and can target common antigens expressed by bacteria (Bunker et al., 2017; Bunker et al., 2015) and (iii) αGal-reactive antibodies present a degree of poly-reactivity against non-αGal related bacterial epitopes (Bernth Jensen et al., 2021).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Bernth Jensen et al. (2021).

claim: The identity of the αGal+ bacteria targeted by IgA likely includes Gram-negative pathobionts from the Enterobacteriaceae family, such as Escherichia coli O86:B7.
source: The identity of the αGal+ bacteria targeted by IgA remains elusive but likely includes Gram-negative pathobionts from the Enterobacteriaceae family, as demonstrated for Escherichia (E.) coli O86:B7 (Yilmaz et al., 2014), which expresses the αGal-like glycan Galα1-3Gal(Fucα1–2)β1-3GlcNAcβ1-4Glc as part of the lipopolysaccharide (LPS) O-antigen (Guo et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Yilmaz et al. (2014) and Guo et al. (2005).

claim: E. coli O86:B7 expresses the αGal-like glycan Galα1-3Gal(Fucα1–2)β1-3GlcNAcβ1-4Glc as part of the lipopolysaccharide (LPS) O-antigen.
source: The identity of the αGal+ bacteria targeted by IgA remains elusive but likely includes Gram-negative pathobionts from the Enterobacteriaceae family, as demonstrated for Escherichia (E.) coli O86:B7 (Yilmaz et al., 2014), which expresses the αGal-like glycan Galα1-3Gal(Fucα1–2)β1-3GlcNAcβ1-4Glc as part of the lipopolysaccharide (LPS) O-antigen (Guo et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Guo et al. (2005).

claim: E. coli O86:B7 can induce a systemic αGal-specific NAb response in humans.
source: Of note, this pathobiont can induce a systemic αGal-specific NAb response in humans (Springer and Horton, 1969) as well as in Ggta1-deleted mice, which is protective against infection by pathogens expressing αGal-like glycans (Yilmaz et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Springer and Horton (1969).

claim: E. coli O86:B7 can induce a systemic αGal-specific NAb response in Ggta1-deleted mice, which is protective against infection by pathogens expressing αGal-like glycans.
source: Of note, this pathobiont can induce a systemic αGal-specific NAb response in humans (Springer and Horton, 1969) as well as in Ggta1-deleted mice, which is protective against infection by pathogens expressing αGal-like glycans (Yilmaz et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Yilmaz et al. (2014).

claim: Several commensal bacteria in the human gut microbiota express αGal-like glycans.
source: The finding that several commensal bacteria in the human gut microbiota express αGal-like glycans (Figure 2—figure supplement 2) suggests that other bacteria might contribute to this protective response.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Ggta1 deletion shapes the bacterial community structure among highly abundant bacterial taxa in the microbiota via an Ig-dependent mechanism, and among low abundant bacterial taxa independently of Ig.
source: Our findings also suggest that Ggta1 deletion shapes the bacterial community structure among highly abundant bacterial taxa in the microbiota via an Ig-dependent mechanism, and among low abundant bacterial taxa independently of Ig (Figure 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Shaping of highly abundant taxa by Ig occurs via a mechanism that involves not only IgA produced by the offspring, but also maternal IgG transferred through the placenta as well as IgM, IgG, and IgA transferred through maternal milk.
source: Presumably, shaping of highly abundant taxa by Ig occurs via a mechanism that involves not only IgA produced by the offspring, but also maternal IgG transferred through the placenta as well as IgM, IgG, and IgA transferred through maternal milk (Koch et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a speculative inference supported by citation to Koch et al. (2016).

claim: Maternal antibodies regulate neonatal innate and adaptive immunity, shaping the offspring microbiota composition.
source: These regulate neonatal innate (Gomez de Agüero et al., 2016) and adaptive (Koch et al., 2016) immunity, shaping the offspring microbiota composition (Gensollen et al., 2016; Koch et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gomez de Agüero et al. (2016), Koch et al. (2016), and Gensollen et al. (2016).

claim: Other mechanisms contribute to shaping the microbiota of Ggta1-deleted mice, including the modulation of nutritional or spatial niches due to the loss of αGal from complex glycosylated structures present at epithelial barriers.
source: Shaping of lowly abundant bacterial taxa independently of Ig (Figure 3) suggests that other mechanisms contribute to shaping the microbiota of Ggta1-deleted mice. These probably include the modulation of nutritional or spatial niches due to the loss of αGal from complex glycosylated structures present at epithelial barriers, such as the mucus, as demonstrated for other glycans (Pickard et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a speculative inference supported by citation to Pickard et al. (2014).

claim: The selective pressure exerted by the adaptive immune system of Ggta1-/- mice on the bacterial species present in the microbiota allows for the establishment of a more diverse ecosystem containing pathobionts.
source: The selective pressure exerted by the adaptive immune system of Ggta1-/- mice on the bacterial species present in the microbiota, probably allows for the establishment of a more diverse ecosystem containing pathobionts (Singh et al., 2021), such as Helicobactereaceae (Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citation to Singh et al. (2021) and data in Figure 1—figure supplements 1 and 2.

claim: Pathobionts in the microbiota can elicit the production of antibodies targeting and exerting negative selective pressure on other bacterial symbionts, releasing ecological niches and further shaping the microbiota.
source: These can elicit the production of antibodies targeting and exerting negative selective pressure on other bacterial symbionts and releasing ecological niches, thus further shaping the microbiota.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about microbiota dynamics.

claim: Expansion of pathobionts in the microbiota of Ggta1-/- mice is restrained by Ig, which explains the lack of associated pathology.
source: Expansion of these pathobionts in the microbiota of Ggta1-/- mice is restrained by Ig, which probably explains the lack of associated pathology (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the enrichment of pathobionts in Ig-deficient mice and the lack of pathology in Ig-sufficient mice, supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

claim: The loss of GGTA1 function in ancestral primates fostered mutualistic interactions with more diverse bacterial ecosystems, incorporating pathobionts such as Helicobacter pylori.
source: This suggests that the loss of GGTA1 function in ancestral primates fostered mutualistic interactions with more diverse bacterial ecosystems, incorporating pathobionts such as Helicobacter pylori, associated with fitness costs (Atherton and Blaser, 2009) and gains (Linz et al., 2007).
evidence: This is a speculative inference about primate evolution supported by citations to Atherton and Blaser (2009) and Linz et al. (2007).

claim: Helicobacter pylori is associated with fitness costs and gains.
source: This suggests that the loss of GGTA1 function in ancestral primates fostered mutualistic interactions with more diverse bacterial ecosystems, incorporating pathobionts such as Helicobacter pylori, associated with fitness costs (Atherton and Blaser, 2009) and gains (Linz et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Atherton and Blaser (2009) and Linz et al. (2007).

claim: Ig-shaping of the bacterial species present in the gut microbiota of Ggta1-/- mice reduces the microbiota pathogenicity.
source: Our findings suggest that Ig-shaping of the bacterial species present in the gut microbiota of Ggta1-/- mice reduces the microbiota pathogenicity, as illustrated when comparing the lethal outcome of systemic infections using the Ig-shaped vs. non-shaped microbiota (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: The effector mechanism underlying resistance against systemic infection by the Ig-shaped microbiota no longer relies on the adaptive immune system but instead on cellular components of the innate immune systems, namely, neutrophils.
source: This reduction in pathogenicity means that the effector mechanism underlying resistance against systemic infection by the Ig-shaped microbiota no longer relies on the adaptive immune system (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and E), but instead on cellular components of the innate immune systems, namely, neutrophils (Figure 4G,H).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and E, and Figure 4G and H.

claim: Ggta1 deletion in mice increases resistance to bacterial sepsis via two distinct antibody-dependent mechanisms: one involving a relative increase in antibody effector function when αGal is not present in the biantennary glycan structures of IgG, and another relying on shaping and reduction of the microbiota pathogenicity by antibodies, most likely from the IgA isotype.
source: We propose that Ggta1 deletion in mice increases resistance to bacterial sepsis via two distinct antibody-dependent mechanisms. The first involves a relative increase in antibody effector function, when αGal is not present in the biantennary glycan structures of IgG (Singh et al., 2021). The second relies on shaping and reduction of the microbiota pathogenicity by antibodies, most likely from the IgA isotype.
evidence: This is a synthesis of findings supported by citation to Singh et al. (2021) and data from the current study.

claim: The notion of host mechanisms shaping the microbiota composition toward a reduction of its pathogenicity is in keeping with host microbial interactions not being hardwired, but instead shifting between symbiotic to pathogenic depending on host and microbe cooperative behaviors.
source: The notion of host mechanisms shaping the microbiota composition toward a reduction of its pathogenicity is in keeping with host microbial interactions not being hardwired, but instead shifting between symbiotic to pathogenic depending on host and microbe cooperative behaviors (Ayres, 2016; Vonaesch et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ayres (2016) and Vonaesch et al. (2018).

claim: When restricted to the microbiota, bacterial pathobionts can behave as commensals, posing no pathogenic threat to the host, while triggering sepsis upon translocation across epithelial barriers.
source: For example, when restricted to the microbiota, bacterial pathobionts can behave as commensals, posing no pathogenic threat to the host (Vonaesch et al., 2018), while triggering sepsis (Haak and Wiersinga, 2017) upon translocation across epithelial barriers (Caruso et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Vonaesch et al. (2018), Haak and Wiersinga (2017), and Caruso et al. (2020).

claim: The high fitness cost imposed to modern humans by sepsis suggests that mutations shaping the composition of the microbiota toward a reduced capacity to elicit sepsis should be associated with major fitness advantages.
source: The high fitness cost imposed to modern humans by sepsis (Rudd et al., 2020) suggests that mutations shaping the composition of the microbiota toward a reduced capacity to elicit sepsis should be associated with major fitness advantages.
evidence: This is an inference based on evolutionary reasoning, supported by citation to Rudd et al. (2020).

claim: Loss-of-function mutations in GGTA1 shape the microbiota toward reduced capacity to elicit sepsis.
source: Our findings suggest that loss-of-function mutations in GGTA1 act in such a manner.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental findings showing reduced microbiota pathogenicity in Ggta1-/- mice.

claim: Non-human primates appear to be far more susceptible to develop sepsis or septic shock when challenged experimentally with a bacterial inoculum or bacterial lipopolysaccharide (LPS), as compared to other mammalian lineages.

claim: Natural selection of traits enhancing immune-driven resistance mechanisms in primates might be associated with lower capacity to establish disease tolerance to infection.
source: One likely explanation for this apparent discrepancy may relate to the intrinsic properties of primate immunity, whereby natural selection of traits enhancing immune-driven resistance mechanisms (Olson, 1999; Wang et al., 2006) might be associated with lower capacity to establish disease tolerance to infection (Martins et al., 2019; Medzhitov et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citations to Olson (1999), Wang et al. (2006), Martins et al. (2019), and Medzhitov et al. (2012).

claim: Resistance and disease tolerance to infection are negatively correlated.
